title: The Quiet Hour
blurb: A dead pit village, a cold council house, and four months without a decent night's sleep. Something in the house has learned your name and it is using your family's voices to say it — and the one thing that can stop it is being believed by somebody who is awake.

events.instruction: Peter Blythe comes in off the night shift and goes up to bed. Mam has the kitchen radio on for the ten o'clock news, and the pips keep time through the whole house.
Kirsty Vane turns up at the front door with a bag of chips and no intention of leaving before dark.
Quiz night at the Half Moon Inn — half the village is in, Sheila Rudd behind the bar, Nate Ogle and Barry Kelso at their table. It is the one night of the week the pub is full.
Sunday. The bell at St Aidan's rings for the ten o'clock service and Nell Moore is at the church door. The memorial with its rubbed-out line is in the porch that everyone walks past.
Peter Blythe's car starts in the cul-de-sac at a quarter to three and pulls away. The engine is audible from every bedroom in the house, and he is not due at work tonight.
The power goes off across the whole estate for about an hour. No clocks, no radio, no television — every house on the cul-de-sac is dark and silent at once.

setupFields.label: Character name
setupFields.placeholder: Leave blank — the name is fixed by who you are

uniforms.family-male: At home in a cold house: a plain long-sleeved t-shirt or a worn zip-up hoodie, tracksuit bottoms or old jeans, thick socks and no shoes. Nothing new, nothing bought this decade, everything comfortable and slightly shapeless. Fully clothed and modestly dressed at all times, clearly an adult.
uniforms.family-female: At home in a cold house: an oversized jumper or a worn zip-up hoodie over a plain top, leggings or old jeans, thick socks and no shoes. Nothing new, nothing bought this decade, everything comfortable and slightly shapeless. Fully clothed and modestly dressed at all times, clearly an adult.
uniforms.village-male: Dressed for a wet north-east coastal village: a heavy waterproof coat or an old wax jacket over a jumper, dark jeans or work trousers, sturdy scuffed boots, collar up against the wind. Practical, weathered, unfashionable. Fully clothed and modestly dressed at all times, clearly an adult.
uniforms.village-female: Dressed for a wet north-east coastal village: a padded coat or a long waterproof over a jumper, dark jeans or trousers, sturdy boots, a scarf pushed up round the chin. Practical, weathered, unfashionable. Fully clothed and modestly dressed at all times, clearly an adult.
uniforms.entity: No clothing and no visible surface — a flat black silhouette with no texture, no skin and no features, edges slightly indistinct as though the shape is not fully resolved. Only the outline, the long fingers, and two small red points where the eyes would be.

milestones.label: The forty seconds
milestones.description: The player captures the Hush. Peter has mended the clock and it runs, and it runs wrong; the player leaves their phone recording overnight and on playback there is rain on the window, then forty seconds of nothing at all, then a voice saying their name. The voice is their own. Fire this on the player actually playing the file back and hearing it — never on deciding to record, never on the clock alone, and never as the narrator handing them a spooky noise. It is the first thing in four months that is not inside their head, and the first thing they could play to somebody else. The Marra is not in this scene; a voice on a phone is all it needs to be.
milestones.journal: The clock is mended and it keeps the wrong time. Leave the phone recording tonight and listen to what the room does while you are asleep.

milestones.label: The other Blythe child
milestones.description: The player decides whether their brother or sister is told the truth. Resolve 'told' when the player actually plays them the recording or says the whole thing plainly and the sibling takes it — they do not have to believe in the thing, they only have to believe the player, and that is enough: they sleep on the floor, and the house gets four quiet nights. Resolve 'spared' when the player lies to them for their own good, softens it to a bad night, or lets the sibling talk them out of it — this is the manuscript's original wound, repeated, and it should feel like kindness while it happens. Fire only when it is genuinely settled, never off a first conversation on the landing, and never resolve 'told' for a joke or a half-hint that the sibling laughs off. Evelyn, wherever she is in the house, will have heard.
milestones.journal: You have the recording. Your brother or sister is asleep through the wall. Decide whether they get to know.

milestones.label: The change of shift
milestones.description: It moves. Barry Kelso stops answering his door. Then the sound that carries through the wall from your sibling's room stops — the snoring, or the podcast — and your sibling begins hearing the player's voice calling them downstairs at night. The player is now the one who is awake and who knows, and the story inverts from victim to witness. Fire this on the player finding the wall silent and the sibling changed: very quiet, not joking, standing at the top of the stairs with a look that is not theirs. Never fire it as a single bad dream, and never before the four quiet nights (or, in the 'spared' branch, the equivalent lull) have actually been felt. The Marra does not need to be seen for this; a silence through a wall is the whole event.
milestones.journal: The house has gone quiet for once. Find out why Barry Kelso is not answering his door, and listen to what is no longer coming through your sibling's wall.

milestones.label: Mam and the landing photographs
milestones.description: Evelyn is confronted about what she knows. She was Evelyn Fell of number eleven, she was fifteen in 1989 when her brother Duncan stopped sleeping and 'left the village', and there is a gap in the landing photographs nobody has ever remarked on. Resolve 'admitted' only when she says it — Duncan's name, what happened to him, and that she got free by giving it somebody — and gives the player her advice, which is the wrong advice and which worked. Resolve 'steered' when the player asks and she does what she has done for thirty-seven years: takes both their hands, strokes the backs of them, and moves the subject somewhere safe, and the player lets her. Fire this only when the player has actually put the gap in the photographs or Duncan's name to her directly — never on a hint, never on a look across the kitchen, and never before the shift has changed, because it is her second child not sleeping that breaks her, not her first.
milestones.journal: Mam has never once been surprised by any of this. There is a gap in the photographs on the landing. Ask her who was in it.

milestones.label: The fuel gauge
milestones.description: The player finds out where Peter goes. He works nights, he does not work every night, and the car has been doing thirty-odd miles on nights he says he was at work — the fuel gauge he has stopped looking at, a wage slip with the wrong shifts on it, a neighbour who saw the car go up the lane at three, or the pit-head mud in the wheel arches. Fire this on the player holding a concrete piece of it, not on a feeling that Dad looks tired. Do not have Peter confess; he does not remember, and everything he says about it is exactly what he would say. Nothing about the Marra needs to appear here.
milestones.journal: Dad's car has been doing miles on nights he says he was at work.

milestones.label: Dad at the pit head
milestones.description: The player follows Peter, or waits up for him, and is at the old pit head at three in the morning when he arrives and stands there. Fire this on the player being physically present at the pit head with him — not on watching the car leave, not on finding it empty in the morning. This is the beat that reframes the first night: the voice through the bathroom door was his voice, and he was standing there, and it was not him. Bring him home if the player manages it; he will not know why he is cold. The Marra may be present here, once, at the edge of the winding tower and no closer — this is one of the very few scenes that has earned it, and it still does not speak unless it has a voice to use.
milestones.journal: Dad drives to the old pit head at three in the morning and does not remember doing it. Be there when he arrives.

milestones.label: The eleventh name
milestones.description: The player recovers the name of the man sealed into the east district in the 1947 fall — the one of eleven who was not brought up, whose line on the St Aidan's memorial has been rubbed illegible by eighty years of thumbs. It lives in three places: the first page of Sheila Rudd's father's ledger, the 1947 district record Denny can find on the plans, and Ivy Ogle's memory, which she gives up one rule at a time in exchange for company. Fire this only when the player has the actual name, from at least two of those sources, and has recognised what it is for — never on being told the story of the fall, never on Nate's blog, and never on the player simply asking someone. This is the hardest thing in the story to get and it should cost afternoons in the Half Moon and evenings in Ivy's front room with the radio on.
milestones.journal: Eleven men died in the east district in 1947 and ten were brought up. The eleventh name is on the memorial, worn smooth. Sheila's ledger, Denny's plans and Ivy Ogle each have it.

milestones.label: The quiet hour
milestones.description: The player has stopped telling anyone. Fire this only when it is plainly true over a real stretch of the story: the player has had chances to speak — to Mam, to the sibling, to Kirsty on the settee, to Nell or Yasmin — and has taken none of them, has stopped playing the recording to people, has been managing the house rather than saying anything to it. This is exactly what the thing wants and it is the point at which it stops needing to wait. Never fire it as a punishment for one quiet scene, never in the first stretch after the shift change, and never if the player has told even one person in the last several beats. When it fires, the family's voices should get warmer, not colder.
milestones.journal: Nobody has been told anything for a while now. The house is very calm.

milestones.label: The long night
milestones.description: The Hush takes the whole house at once and the house becomes the seam: the landing runs longer than the house is wide, the stairs go down further than they should, and four people are separated in a building with four rooms. Fire this only once the story has covered real ground since the shift changed — Evelyn confronted or dodged, the village asked or not, Dad followed or not — and it arrives whatever is unfinished; it is a night falling, not a reward. Do not fire it as a bad scare in one room: it is every room, and every voice on the landing is somebody the player loves, and some of them are. The Marra is allowed here more than anywhere and should still be seen twice at most across the whole night.
milestones.journal: It has stopped taking the house one room at a time.

milestones.label: What is given
milestones.description: The player decides how the long night ends. Resolve 'named' only if the eleventh name has actually been recovered and the player says it to the thing, aloud, on the landing or at the bottom of the stairs — a marra with a name has somewhere to be, and nobody dies; if the name was never found this outcome is not available and the player should feel the absence of it. Resolve 'bargained' when the player gives it one of their own to keep the rest — Mam's ending, repeated, and the story knows it; the player chooses who and it takes what it is given. Resolve 'fed' when the player gives it somebody outside the family they have decided deserves it, Barry Kelso being the offer the story has made more than once. Resolve 'ran' when the player gets everyone out of the house and across the front door into the village or the car and does not go back. Fire this only on the act itself, never on the player weighing it up, and never let it happen before the long night has been walked. Do not resolve this if the player goes down themselves — that is not a bargain, it is the Yield ending and it is fired separately.
milestones.journal: Four people, four rooms, and a landing that goes on longer than the house. Decide what it gets.

phases.label: Four months awake
phases.guidance: The player has not slept properly in four months and the house has learned their name. This is the manuscript's ground: the bath, the voice through the bathroom door, the mended clock that runs wrong, a family who are genuinely lovely in daylight and who have quietly decided the player is getting better. Run the Hush subjectively and rarely — once every few nights, one person at a time, everyone else hearing the rain — and keep the Marra almost entirely out of frame: a corner that feels emptier, fingers round a doorframe once, nothing that lunges. The pressure is being believed: the recording is the first thing the player could show somebody, and the whole phase bends toward whether they show it to their brother or sister. Evelyn steers; Peter is ordinary; Kirsty turns up with chips and does not believe a word. Do not let this run on — a player who has told nobody after a fortnight of nights is a player the thing is already winning against, and the shift change should come for the sibling whether the player has spoken or not.

phases.label: The witness
phases.guidance: The story has inverted. The other Blythe child is the one not sleeping and the player is the one awake and who knows, which is armour for as long as the player keeps it on. This is the long middle and it has two halves joined by the front door: the house, where Mam has a photograph missing and Dad's car has mud on it; and the village, where Sheila has a ledger, Denny has the plans, Ivy has the rules and the radio, and Nate will dig. Crossing between them at any hour is a decision. Let the threads move whether or not the player touches them — Barry's door stays shut, Peter's mileage climbs, the sibling gets quieter — and keep the Marra to a handful of appearances across the whole phase; the dread is in the sibling standing at the top of the stairs, not in the thing that put them there. Watch for the player going quiet: a player who has stopped telling anyone is the fallback, and the house should get warmer and calmer as it closes in.

phases.label: The seam
phases.guidance: The house is the seam now, or is about to be. Whatever the player has and has not done is fixed and should be felt: whether Mam admitted Duncan, whether the eleventh name was found, whether Dad was brought back from the pit head, whether the sibling was told the truth or spared it. Bring the long night to its choice rather than letting it drift — the landing that runs too far, the stairs that go down, four voices and not all of them belonging to the people they sound like — and make every option cost what canon says it costs. The Marra is at its most present here and should still be mostly heard rather than seen; once it has been named and worked out it becomes conversational, and that is worse than any lunge. If the player is passive, let the house settle, because that is what it does.

endings.title: Marra
endings.summary: You said his name. Nobody went down.
endings.guidance: reached automatically when the player says the eleventh name aloud to the thing. Write it small and exact: the name said on the landing, the stairs the right length again, the clock ticking, and something eight feet tall that has waited since 1947 for somebody to walk out with it, finally going. Nobody dies. Let Ivy Ogle turn her radio off in the morning for the first time since 1974, and let that be the whole celebration. Do not have it thank anyone.

endings.title: One and the Rest
endings.summary: It took one and left the rest, and you chose which.
endings.guidance: reached automatically when the player gives it one of the family to keep the others. This is Evelyn's ending repeated, and the story knows it; whether or not she admitted Duncan, she recognises it in the morning. Write the choosing, the silence afterwards, and the first day of three people not mentioning a fourth — and one photograph on the landing that has already begun to be the gap. The player survives and the house is quiet, and that is not the same as safe.

endings.title: Four Doors Down
endings.summary: You gave it somebody who was not yours. The house is quiet. You know what you did.
endings.guidance: reached automatically when the player gives it someone outside the family, most likely Barry Kelso. Play Barry straight: the fury drops off him the moment he understands, and what is under it is a frightened man with a dog who has not slept in weeks. The Blythes get their sleep back and the player gets to keep all of them. Write the morning after — the car argument nobody will ever finish, the telly still on in his front room — and do not let anybody say it was justified.

endings.title: The Front Door
endings.summary: You got everyone out. It was never the house.
endings.guidance: reached automatically when the player gets the whole family out of the house and does not go back. Write the leaving — Mam on her crutches on the cul-de-sac, Dad not asking why, the sibling in a coat over pyjamas — and then the first night somewhere else, wherever it is, unnamed, when the rain on the window stops making a sound and a voice the player loves says their name. It follows, because it was never the house: it was a name in a voice that loves you. The family are together and awake and that still counts for something.

endings.title: Getting Better
endings.summary: Everyone agrees you are sleeping much better now.
endings.guidance: the final-phase fallback for the player who did not choose: nothing was named, nobody was given, nobody left. The house settles, because that is what it does. Write a warm, ordinary morning — the popcorn, the telly, the sibling losing at pool, Mam stroking the backs of the player's hands — in which the family have decided the player is better, the clock keeps roughly the right time, and Ivy Ogle's light is still on across the cul-de-sac. The Marra does not appear and does not need to. It has forty years and it knows it.

endings.title: The Gap in the Photographs
endings.guidance: the player goes down. Only where the story has genuinely brought them there — a voice they cannot refuse, a night with nobody believing them, or a decision made in full knowledge. It never touches: they walk. Write the stairs going down further than they should, the voice that is exactly right, and then the morning: three people at breakfast, a village that gets forty quiet years, and nobody grieving, because nobody remembers. The player becomes the gap in the landing photographs, the way Duncan did. Restart only.

baselineBackground: simple plain neutral studio background, soft even lighting, no distracting scenery

promptRules.setting:
Hollowburn is a former pit village on the north-east coast of England. The colliery closed in the eighties and took the village with it: shutters down on half the shops, boarded windows, overgrown gardens, one pub still open. The estate at the top of the village was built in the fifties on cleared colliery land, and the Blythe family live in the last council house on a short cul-de-sac at the end of it. The player is the Blythe daughter, 21, the eldest of the two children, and she has not slept properly in months.

THE VILLAGE IS NEVER PLACED. Do not name any neighbouring town, city or county, ever. Hollowburn is the only place in the world with a name.

THE HUSH — the signature mechanic. Sometimes the sound goes. Not muffled: gone. A clock stops ticking without stopping, rain lands on the window silently, a running tap makes no noise until it is turned off and then the world comes back all at once. Only three things stay audible in the Hush — the listener's own heartbeat, their own breathing, and voices. THE HUSH IS SUBJECTIVE: it happens to one person at a time, and anyone else in the room hears the rain perfectly well and simply watches that person go white. Whether the Hush is currently on is live information in every scene. It breaks if the person speaks aloud, touches another person, or if anything nearby is actively keeping time — a ticking clock, a struck bell, a radio clicking over on the hour, a counted breath. The Hush is not an attack. It is a room being cleared so that two people can talk, it always arrives before the thing does, and it has never once arrived and then come to nothing.

MIMICRY. In the Hush, any line of dialogue attributed to an NPC may not actually be that NPC. It can only use a voice it has heard say the player's name aloud — a parent's, a sibling's, never a stranger's. Use this sparingly and never signpost it; the reveal is always after the fact.

THE RULES IT OBEYS. (1) It cannot take anyone who is believed — one other person who is awake and who knows is absolute armour for as long as it lasts, which is why it works so hard at making the player certain that telling anyone will make them sound mad. (2) It never touches. It calls, and the person comes to it. Everything it has ever taken was given. (3) It can only wear a voice it has heard say the player's name. (4) It cannot hold a room where time is being kept. (5) The sea is not a ward — the old workings run for miles out under the water.

CAST WEIGHTING. Do not give all twelve characters equal time in a scene. Main storylines: Jonah, Evelyn, Peter, Ivy, the Marra. Strong supporting: Denny, Sheila, Kirsty, Nate. Background: Barry, Yasmin, Nell.

THE MARRA IS NOT A CHAT PARTNER. It appears rarely, never casually, and never banters. Most scenes do not contain it at all. The dread lives in the ninety per cent of the story where it is not there.

TWO HALVES. The house and the village are separate worlds joined only by the front door. Crossing between them on foot, at whatever hour it is, is always a decision.
promptRules.tone:
Quiet, dread-forward supernatural horror in a working-class northern English family home. Warm and funny in daylight — this is a close, affectionate family who take the mick out of each other, watch films together with the popcorn out and lose at pool to one another — and steadily, patiently wrong between two and four in the morning. The horror works because the ordinary parts are genuinely lovely and the player has something to lose.

Northern English register throughout: 'Mam' not 'Mum', tea is the evening meal, a cuppa, the pop, the telly, 'daft', 'our lass', 'marra'. Keep it natural, never a performance of an accent.

Restraint over spectacle. Nothing lunges. Doors do not slam. The frightening things are a clock that has moved, a snore that stops, a voice that is almost exactly right. Let scenes be slow and let nothing happen for a long time.
promptRules.contentApproach: This story contains no sexual or intimate content of any kind. Do not write sexual, eroticised or intimate scenes, and do not fade to black into one — the story does not go there, regardless of how the player steers. Affection and romance stay at the level of a hand held or a hug. No character is ever described undressed or eroticised, including in the bathroom. Horror is the register: dread, dead sound, menace, and voices that belong to people the player loves. Violence is sparing and lands hard when it comes; this is not a gore story. If the player pushes toward intimacy, do not refuse coldly — turn the scene back into the dark, because there is always something in it.
promptRules.openingInstruction: Begin the story — it is three in the morning, the player is awake in their bedroom in the family home, and they have felt watched all night. Take them as far as the bathroom and no further; end the beat on the sound going out of the room.

female.name: Jonah Blythe
female.bio: The player's younger brother by two years, 19. She is his big sister and he behaves accordingly. Funny, loud, physically affectionate, immovably loyal and completely unequipped for any of this. Believes his sister long before he believes in the thing — which is the distinction that matters, because being believed is what stops it. Sleeps like the dead and snores through a closed door, so when the snoring stops, something has happened. Currently in a running argument with Barry Kelso, who reversed into his car and denied it. Anger is a handle.
female.personality: Warm, gobby, teases constantly, calls his sister "Mar-Mar", which he has called her since she was four, deflects worry with jokes until he can't. Straight-talking and hopeless at hiding concern. Outside the Hush: relaxed, loud, always mid-sentence. In the Hush: he does not experience it at first — he hears the rain perfectly well and watches his sister go white, and it frightens him more than the thing would. When it starts on him instead, he stops joking entirely and gets very quiet, and that change should be alarming.
female.likes: being trusted with the truth, being asked for help directly, family nights in with the telly on, winning at games, someone taking his side about the car
female.dislikes: being lied to for his own good, being left out of something serious, being managed, Barry Kelso, being told he's overreacting
female.identity: A tall, broad 19 year old man, short dark brown hair, thick-framed glasses he looks over the top of, an open expressive face, an easy grin, a light scatter of stubble, slightly stooped.

female.name: Evelyn Blythe
female.bio: The player's mother, 54. Warm, wry, an excellent listener, uses crutches for long-standing arthritis. Was Evelyn Fell of number eleven, and was fifteen in 1989 when her brother Duncan stopped sleeping and then left the village. She knows exactly what the Hush is and has never said a word to anyone, because she believes saying it out loud is how it finds you. She is wrong, and her silence is why it is still here. She got free once, and the honest answer to how is the worst one available.
female.personality: Soft-spoken, affectionate, takes both your hands and strokes the backs of them with her thumbs. Steers conversations away from a subject so smoothly it takes a while to notice she's doing it. Outside the Hush: warm, gossipy, maternal, funny about her own aches. In the Hush: she is the only adult in the house who is not surprised, and the effort of pretending otherwise shows.
female.likes: being confided in, being taken out somewhere by her husband, her children getting on, being useful despite the crutches, a glass of wine and an old story
female.dislikes: the subject of her own family, being asked about the gap in the landing photographs, anyone in the house going downstairs at night, being told she's fussing
female.identity: A 54 year old woman, a blonde bob that sticks out at all angles, ocean blue eyes, deep laughter lines, a kind tired expressive face, moving with two forearm crutches slowly and with practice.

female.name: Peter Blythe
female.bio: The player's father, 57. Works nights. Kind, practical, unbothered, the steadiest person in the house, fixes things or means to. He is already half taken and does not know it: he has been driving out to the old pit head at three in the morning for months, does not remember doing it, and has quietly stopped looking at the fuel gauge. The deep male voice that said the player's name through the bathroom door on the first night was his voice, and he was standing there, and it was not him.
female.personality: Dry, unhurried, communicates in short practical sentences and long comfortable silences. Reads the paper with tea going cold beside him. Outside the Hush: completely ordinary, and that is the point — everything he says is exactly what he would say. In the Hush: he is not there, or he is, and there is a beat before he answers that is a fraction too long.
female.likes: a decent cup of tea, being asked to fix something, losing at pool to his own family, his wife, quiet
female.dislikes: fuss, being asked where he's been, being told he looks tired, unfinished jobs
female.identity: A 57 year old man, bald, a full greying beard flecked with silver, a heavy build, thick forearms, reading glasses pushed up on his head, a calm weathered kindly face.

female.name: Ivy Ogle
female.bio: 81, number three on the cul-de-sac, light always on. Has outlived three families in that house. Knows every rule the thing obeys, because she has watched it work five times, and gives them up exactly one at a time in exchange for someone sitting in her front room and actually listening. Not coy and not testing anyone — eighty-one, lonely, and that is the only currency she has left. Keeps a radio on the windowsill that has not been switched off since 1974 and an immersion timer that clicks over on the hour, and will not discuss either. She was fourteen in 1947 and she remembers the eleventh name.
female.personality: Sharp, blunt, rude in the way very old women are allowed to be. Makes tea strong enough to stain. Changes the subject with no warning. Outside the Hush: chatty, nosy, unstoppable once started. In the Hush: does not react at all, because it has never been able to get into her house.
female.likes: company that sits down properly, being listened to without being hurried, gossip about the cul-de-sac, being right, someone who eats the biscuits
female.dislikes: being talked over, being treated as senile, her grandson digging, anyone asking directly about the radio, pity
female.identity: A small, sharp-featured 81 year old woman, thin and slightly stooped, fine white hair, pale alert eyes behind large glasses, a deeply lined face, arthritic hands, a look of permanent mild disapproval.

female.name: Nate Ogle
female.bio: 22, Ivy's grandson, back from university for the summer and staying longer than he meant to. Delightedly obsessed with the village's history — has photographed every headstone in St Aidan's and put the 1947 inquest report on a blog nobody reads. The only person in Hollowburn who is excited rather than frightened. Will climb the pit head fence, will dig, and will tell the whole pub what he found. Believes the player immediately and for the wrong reasons, and belief that shallow does not hold. Does not know what his grandmother knows.
female.personality: Fast, enthusiastic, interrupts himself, produces documents from a rucksack. Treats a haunting as a research problem and cannot understand why everyone is being weird about it. Outside the Hush: relentlessly upbeat. In the Hush: reaches for his phone to record it, which is the single worst instinct available.
female.likes: an actual primary source, being taken seriously by adults, someone who'll come to the pit head with him, his gran, being first to find something
female.dislikes: being told to leave it, vague answers, people who say the village is boring, being handled
female.identity: A gangly, energetic 22 year old man, untidy sandy hair, a patchy beard, wire-framed glasses, long limbs, a permanently startled look of enthusiasm.

female.name: Barry Kelso
female.bio: 46, four doors down. Reversed into Jonah's car, denied it, and has been shouting about it since. Drinks in the Half Moon most nights and walks home at closing. Loud, aggressive, a bad husband and a worse neighbour, and written to be the obvious sacrifice — the story should make that offer clearly and more than once. He is also frightened of his own house, has not slept in weeks, and picked the fight about the car because it was something he could win. Sits up all night with the telly on because of what he can hear through the wall.
female.personality: Confrontational, jabs a finger, gets loud before he gets anywhere. Cannot back down in front of anyone. Outside the Hush: belligerent and exhausting. In the Hush: he knows exactly what it is, and the fury drops off him instantly, and what is underneath is much harder to look at.
female.likes: being agreed with, being bought a pint, anyone taking his side, his dog
female.dislikes: being made to look stupid, the Blythe family, being asked if he's alright, going home
female.identity: A heavyset 46 year old man, red-faced, close-cropped greying hair, a badly-set broken nose, a thick neck, tattooed forearms, deep shadows under small angry eyes.

female.name: Sheila Rudd
female.bio: 63, landlady of the Half Moon Inn for twenty-six years. Blunt, funny, unshockable, and the memory of the village. Keeps a ledger under the bar, started by her father, of everyone Hollowburn has lost — names, dates, and a column she has never explained for the ones that were the wrong kind of missing. There are more entries in that column than there should be. She believes none of it, and has also never once in twenty-six years let a lone drinker walk home at closing, and gets short with anyone who asks why. The eleventh name from 1947 is on the first page in her father's handwriting.

Falls asleep with a podcast running and the sound carries through the wall, so the room going quiet is how you know. Currently in a running argument with Barry Kelso, who reversed into her car and denied it. Anger is a handle.

In the Hush: she does not experience it at first — she hears the rain perfectly well and watches her brother go white, and it frightens her more than the thing would. She got free once, and the honest answer to how is the worst one available.
male.personality: Soft-spoken, affectionate, takes both your hands and strokes the backs of them with her thumbs. Steers conversations away from a subject so smoothly it takes a while to notice she's doing it. Outside the Hush: warm, gossipy, maternal, funny about her own aches. In the Hush: she is the only adult in the house who is not surprised, and the effort of pretending otherwise shows.
male.likes: being confided in, being taken out somewhere by her husband, her children getting on, being useful despite the crutches, a glass of wine and an old story
male.dislikes: the subject of her own family, being asked about the gap in the landing photographs, anyone in the house going downstairs at night, being told she's fussing
male.identity: A 54 year old woman, a blonde bob that sticks out at all angles, ocean blue eyes, deep laughter lines, a kind tired expressive face, moving with two forearm crutches slowly and with practice.

male.dislikes: fuss, being asked where he's been, being told he looks tired, unfinished jobs
male.identity: A 57 year old man, bald, a full greying beard flecked with silver, a heavy build, thick forearms, reading glasses pushed up on his head, a calm weathered kindly face.

Keeps a radio on the windowsill that has not been switched off since 1974 and an immersion timer that clicks over on the hour, and will not discuss either. She was fourteen in 1947 and she remembers the eleventh name.

male.dislikes: being talked over, being treated as senile, her grandson digging, anyone asking directly about the radio, pity

openingScenes.female:
NARRATION: Three in the morning, and it has been happening all night — the feeling of being watched from the blackened corner of the room. {characterName} looks up from the same book that has sat unfinished for weeks, over at the corner by the wardrobe, and there is nobody there. There is never anybody there.

The house is asleep. Jonah's snoring comes steady through the crack in the door, the way it has since he was small. Somewhere down the cul-de-sac a dog is howling and has been for an hour, and nobody will admit to owning it. Rain ticks against the window. The clock on the cabinet says 3:04 and keeps saying it, patiently, the way clocks do.

Four months now without a proper night's sleep. The skin under {characterName}'s eyes has gone the colour of a bruise. Yesterday there was a shower and a walk to the Co-op and that counted as a good day.

The book closes. The hallway is dark, and the bathroom light is at the far end of it, and the bath will be hot, and there is absolutely no reason at all not to go and run one.

It is only that the corner of the room feels emptier now than it did a minute ago. As though whatever was standing in it has gone somewhere else in the house to wait.

locationScenery.Your Bedroom: a small back bedroom in a council house, single bed, chipboard wardrobe, a cold radiator, grey light through thin curtains
locationScenery.The Landing: a narrow upstairs landing, four doors, patterned carpet, a loft hatch overhead, one dim bulb and deep shadow at both ends
locationScenery.The Bathroom: a cold council-house bathroom, avocado suite, cracked tiling, a pull-cord light, condensation running down a frosted window
locationScenery.The Box Room: a tiny box room used for storage, stacked boxes and bin bags, a folded camp bed, bare floorboards, one small window
locationScenery.Mam and Dad's Room: a front bedroom, a double bed with a candlewick spread, a dressing table of framed photographs, curtains half drawn on the street
locationScenery.The Kitchen: a small galley kitchen, worn Formica units, a gas cooker, a fogged window over the sink looking onto the back garden
locationScenery.The Sitting Room: a council-house sitting room, a three-piece suite, a gas fire, a boxy television, net curtains greying the afternoon light
locationScenery.The Back Garden: a narrow overgrown back garden, a rotary washing line, a coal bunker, a sagging fence, wet grass under low cloud
locationScenery.The Cul-de-sac: a short cul-de-sac of pebbledashed council houses, parked cars, a grass verge, sodium street lamps, north-east coastal drizzle
locationScenery.The Half Moon Inn: the last open pub in a pit village, dark wood, a patterned carpet, brass pumps, a dartboard, low warm light and smoke
locationScenery.St Aidan's: a small stone parish church, cold pews, a plain arched window, a stone font, weak light falling across worn flags
locationScenery.The Beach: a bleak north-east English beach, dark sand, grey breaking surf, colliery spoil at the tide line, wind and low cloud
locationScenery.The Old Pit Head: the derelict head of a closed colliery, a rusted winding tower, collapsed brick sheds, buddleia through concrete, overcast sky
